speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) what is Singapore’s inflation outlook in the near and medium terms; (b) what are the causes of the rising inflationary pressures; (c) what is the assessment of the likely impact of these inflationary pressures on low and middle income households; and (d) whether there will be mitigating measures to reduce the impact of rising costs arising from these inflationary pressures on households and businesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) whether the Ministry can provide an update on the risk of a sharp accumulation of external and domestic cost pressures affecting prices of goods and services in Singapore; and (b) other than tighter monetary policy, what steps can be taken to mitigate some of the effects of rising costs over the next 12 months.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Speaker, Sir, with your permission, can I take Question Nos 5 and 6 together, please?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The rise in domestic inflation came largely on the back of higher external inflation due to increases in global energy and food commodity prices, and persistent supply bottlenecks in key global industries and transport hubs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On the energy front, crude oil prices have risen to above US$80 per barrel since early October on account of the decision by OPEC+ to keep supply increases modest, even as oil demand continues to pick up due to the global economic recovery and the rally in global natural gas prices.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Higher oil and gas prices will translate to higher electricity prices domestically.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And about 95% of our electricity is currently generated using natural gas.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On the food front, global prices for food commodities such as cereals and vegetable oil have risen due to supply constraints arising from weather-related disruptions, manpower and labour shortages and export restrictions in key food-producing countries, amidst rising global demand.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Higher global food prices will in turn, naturally, exert upward pressure on domestic food prices.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks for goods such as semiconductors, and congestion at ports around the world, have contributed to a rise in the prices of imported consumer goods in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Domestically, we expect labour costs to rise as the labour market continues to recover and border restrictions limit non-resident worker inflow.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We also expect to see inflation in accommodation to persist due to strong rental demand for housing amidst construction delays caused by labour shortages in the construction sector.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But despite this rise in inflation, Singapore’s economic recovery for the year remains on track.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Barring a major setback in the global economy, GDP growth is expected to come in between 6% and 7% for the full year, mainly supported by outward-oriented sectors, such as the manufacturing, finance and insurance, and information and communications sectors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Government recognises that higher inflation is a cause of concern for Singaporeans, particularly those in lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: To manage the cost of living pressures faced by Singaporeans, the Government adopts a multi-pronged approach.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: A strong Singapore dollar will help to mitigate imported inflation and temper domestic cost, to ensure price stability over the medium term.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Second, the Government strives to maintain and manage domestic supply-side constraints, and these include the supply of industrial and commercial spaces to help moderate business cost increases, and reduce the knock-on impact on consumer prices.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: During the pandemic, the Government has also disbursed rental relief to help businesses cope with their rental costs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In addition, policy measures, such as the Wage Credit Scheme, Jobs Support Scheme and Jobs Growth Incentive Scheme, provide some support for businesses in terms of their manpower and labour costs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Third, to mitigate the impact of rising global food prices, the Government has diversified our food import sources to help ensure that the prices of our food supplies remain competitive.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Fourth, we will continue to pay particular attention to Singaporeans from lower-income households who need support for their basic living expenses.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Government will continue to provide assistance through ComCare and the permanent GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: From time to time, the Government also introduces one-off support measures, such as the Budget 2020 Grocery Vouchers Scheme.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In addition, Singaporeans from lower- to middle-income households who have experienced involuntary job or income loss due to the economic impact of COVID-19 can apply for financial assistance provided through schemes, such as the COVID-19 Recovery Grant and the Courage Fund.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Government will continue to monitor inflation and cost of living pressures closely and adjust our policies where necessary.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have just one supplementary question and somewhat related to Question No 5 as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond the mitigation measures that the Minister of State mentioned just now – we are thankful for the support for expenses and other mitigation measures – can he give an update on other pre-emptive efforts?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, the Retail Price Watch Group (RPWG).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: An update on that would be quite useful.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Slightly more than a decade ago, we created that to keep a watch on retail prices and address concerns on any alleged profiteering and excessive pricing of daily necessities and food items.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And the role of cooperation with retailers going forward, as a price stabiliser, I think that element of pre-emptive efforts might be useful at this point in time as we proceed into 2022.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we can have further updates from the Minister of State, please.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Government maintains a very strong vigilant stance on price increases and price fluctuations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For daily necessities, consumers can make use of CASE's Price Kaki app to compare prices of groceries and hawker food to help them to make more informed purchasing decisions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But as I have mentioned earlier on, I wanted to just reinforce that it is a whole multi-prong approach, a broad and expansive approach that the Government is taking to tackle inflation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We have mentioned earlier on MAS' monetary policy adjustments, the Government managing supply-site constraints, which is not unique to Singapore but globally.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Our approach has been wide and expansive and broad to help our people to cope with inflation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister of State whether there is further scope for our strong Singapore dollar to mitigate imported inflation, given that it does impact our export competitiveness; whether, from our trade consideration standpoint, is there further room for that to be used to mitigate imported inflation?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Minister of State also mentioned about the push for higher wages, the additional measures from the COVID-19-related safe management procedures that the businesses got to follow, the energy prices and others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My concern is whether all these upward pressures on cost will lead to businesses pricing in this anticipated increase in cost and, therefore, will create a spiral in inflation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister of State how the Government is going to manage this, whether there will be interventions and also for items that are outside the CPI basket, how are we going to mitigate those cost increases as well.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As we all know, inflation is a clear and present issue confronting and vexing economists this week, as well as central bankers and policy-makers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: South Korea just announced that inflation hit a 10-year high in October.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As I earlier updated, MAS had already made a decisive move on 14 October by raising the slope of the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It had also said that it would continue to track the growth and inflation trajectories over the next few quarters.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is one tool in the toolbox; there are many others.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And maybe I will just share with the Member how we are dealing with inflationary issues.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If you look at the thing as a whole, this issue has been more acute because of two major challenges.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The first is that the supply-side constraints and the second is an economic rebound.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The supply-side constraints have been in place, pre-COVID-19, but accentuated during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The economic pick-up will lead to pent-up demand, economic rebounding, and so, you have huge demand but then, continued supply constraints.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If you look at what is happening right now, despite all of these input prices, our exports have in fact seen a very strong recovery this year.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This NODX growth in Q3 2021 was driven mainly by exports of non-electronic products such as specalised machinery, petrochemicals and pharmaceuticals.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: When our export performance is strong, it means also that our exports remain competitive in international markets.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And we must keep these markets open so that our goods can flow out.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It also manages a hedge against other price increases, inbound.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: At the same time, the other way to manage this is to ensure that our supply chains remain connected and that means diversifying our import and export markets.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We have and are negotiating, and have successfully concluded negotiations on the Pacific Alliance Singapore Free Trade Agreement.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is another arrow in our quiver such that we can open up new markets for our imports to alleviate, again, inflationary pressures.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will also continue to support local enterprises so they can deepen their export capabilities in the global economy and ensure our exports remain relevant and competitive in the international market in the long term.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The other aspects to reduce inflationary pressures include also the supply of industrial and commercial spaces to help moderate business costs and reduce the knock-on impact on consumer prices.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These also include measures such as disbursing rental relief to help businesses cope with their rental costs and, hopefully, have knock-on effects to consumers as well.
